title: Why Does an Hour Have 60 Minutes?

fin.big: Simplified illustrations. Facts checked against published histories.
fin.small: Sources: O. Neugebauer, The Exact Sciences in Antiquity (1969); al-Biruni, The Chronology of Ancient Nations (Sachau transl., 1879)

parts: Why does an hour have sixty minutes, not a hundred? Blame people from four thousand years ago.
Stay to hear what the word second really means.
In ancient Sumer, in what is now Iraq, people counted in sixties.
Babylon kept it for math and the stars.
Why sixty? Nobody is sure. But sixty splits cleanly into halves, thirds, quarters, fifths and sixths.
But here is the odd part. The first known split of the hour into sixty came much later.
Around the year one thousand, the scholar al Biruni split hours into minutes and seconds.
Then he kept going, into thirds and fourths.
In Latin, a minute was the first small part.
And a second was the second small part. That is the whole name.
One historian credits a later scholar with making it a system.
Our reading: your phone still counts time like Babylon. Subscribe for the next one.
